extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, psychologists, philosophers of science, and students interested in the cognitive processes of mathematical discovery
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how different mental representations (words, images, algebraic signs, diagrams) and stages of consciousness contribute to mathematical thought, invention, and the process of discovery. Discusses individual differences, incubation, verification, and the roles of notation and imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-verbal thought / absence of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is often not accompanied by words; for some (Galton, the author) words disappear at the moment of real thinking and only reappear when trying to express results in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galton's statement: inability to think in words is a serious drawback for writing and explaining — one must 'translate' thoughts into language, causing wasted time and obscurity in spontaneous speech. The page gives first-person examples (difficulty lecturing on anything but mathematical subjects without writing nearly every part down) and notes that words may be entirely absent even for algebraic signs in difficult reasoning. Anti-pattern: assuming everyone thinks in words as Max Müller does; this misconception can lead to polemics rather than inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental pictures / imagery accompany thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought can be accompanied by concrete representations other than words — recurring, surviving sensations or images that resurge with ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taine's, Galton's, and Binet's observations are cited; Binet's experimental introspections show images can appear as sudden feelings, sometimes minimizing intervention of imagery in controlled questioning. Examples include children and women having finer images, and descriptions of how images may cut or accompany thought. Use: images help give a synthesis or gestalt of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of thought types: free vs controlled vs tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychologists distinguish free (wandering) thought, controlled thought (directed to a goal), and tense thought (concentrated inventive effort); these types differ in their mental accompaniments and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that tense (inventive) thought requires concentrated effort and behaves differently than free or merely controlled thought; many experimental results (Binet, Dwelshauvers) concern controlled but not tense thought, so one must be cautious extrapolating. The tense thought case is the one that directly concerns mathematical invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words/images can give precision to vague unconscious ideas (Binet's view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words or sensorimotor images may be useful to give a precise form to feelings/thoughts that otherwise would remain vague and unconscious, allowing passage from unconscious to conscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binet concludes that words/images can help make unconscious ideas precise and conscious, but the author warns this may risk altering the original unconscious idea: 'giving precision to unconscious ideas would always risk altering them.' Use cautiously: helpful for making ideas explicit, but can change them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vague, schematic mental imagery for synthesis (avoid deceptive precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective mental schemata for mathematical synthesis are characteristically vague schematic images (not precise depictions) which hold the whole and permit manipulation without misleading about properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Euler's circle diagrams, a vague 'confused mass' and a point beyond it in the proof of infinitely many primes, ribbons indicating where dominant terms lie. Vague images satisfy the need to keep links together without supplying inaccurate detailed properties (condition (b) in author's argument). Anti-pattern: precise unconscious imagery that suggests incorrect properties (dangerous for arithmetic/algebraic reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor between full-consciousness and fringe-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-consciousness focuses on successive images or the global image; the detailed arguments or steps may remain waiting in a kind of 'antechamber' (fringe-consciousness) which supplies support when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reports that during concentrated work the consciousness is on images while the logical arguments are 'in the antechamber'; fringe-consciousness is at service of full-consciousness and can present representations when required. This division explains the utility of vague images/schemes and how verification/precising stages follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubation and illumination (unconscious contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods of incubation involve deeper unconscious processes that can produce sudden illumination; such results may be transmitted to consciousness as symbolic or schematic diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author conjectures an unconscious mechanism that satisfies conditions of being both useful and non-deceptive; examples include sudden schematic visualizations recalled from earlier work (author's 1892 visualization) and the role of fringe-consciousness in representing illumination. After illumination follows verifying and precising stage, often involving algebraic symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relay-results / intermediate verified formulas to stabilize progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate verified results (relay-results) provide stability to intellectual progress and serve as new starting points for further advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such relay-results, one may find previously arranged symbolic dispositions 'dead' on resuming work and must often begin anew; verified formulas permit continuation across interruptions. William Hamilton's comparison (progress as tending through a sand-bank) illustrates necessity of establishing each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams and visual representations aid reasoning despite formal eliminability
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams and geometric visual sense frequently guide mathematicians even when formal logic eliminates the need for concrete pictures (e.g., Hilbert's axiomatic geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's formal elimination of geometrical sense didn't prevent his use of geometric intuition while developing rigorous foundations; diagrams appear widely (even in Hilbert's book) and help synthesis without compromising logical rigor. Euler's diagrammatic representation of syllogisms and relay-results in geometry are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic-visual thought: words seen as printed images
rubrics_metrics.description: Some individuals experience ideas in the form of printed words (typographic-visual type) rather than pictorial or auditory images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ribot's cases: a physiologist who saw words like 'dog' or chemical symbols as printed; such persons may find it hard to conceive other modes of thought. This is a distinct cognitive style that affects how one conceives the relation between language and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditory mental imagery influences writing and causes errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory images (sounds of words or rhythms) can dominate thought for some and lead to automatic-writing errors where similar-sounding words are substituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives personal examples: while writing, auditory confusions produced words like 'simple' instead of 'sameplace' or 'willshe' instead of 'we shall.' Note: such auditory mistakes may be more frequent in a non-native language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental use of algebraic symbols vs avoidance in difficult thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mathematicians think in algebraic symbols (visualizing the symbols), while others avoid precise algebraic signs during hard thinking and use vague schematic representations instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: G. D. Birkhoff visualizes algebraic symbols; many others use vague images. The author notes that algebraic symbols may be used for easy calculations but become 'too heavy' in more difficult matters; when precise notation is present externally (on blackboard) the mental schema may disappear and be replaced by the explicit formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper notation and word choice can fix and aid recall of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly chosen notation or the 'right word' can illuminate the situation, fix an idea in the mind, and help recall mathematical concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polya's observation: a proper letter choice can give similar help; he taught students mnemonics linking letters (z for Zahl, w for Wert). The 'right word' or notation can be subtly appropriate and serve as a mnemonic or clarifying device. Use: deliberately choose notation/labels to help synthesis and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination focuses attention and coordinates multiple deductions (Descartes' idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing imagination on the object to be considered prevents its wandering and can be useful in awakening certain ideas and in coordinating several deductions whose results must be integrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes' view (via Boutroux) that imagination, though not creating science alone, can be useful for focusing and coordinating many deductions. This supports keeping an image of problem data present to avoid forgetting and to permit their use at each instant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of equating words with ideas (words as misleading labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equating words with ideas can be dangerous: words may function like paper money (useful but risky), and reliance on words alone may produce misunderstandings or paralogisms in reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author criticizes Max Müller's claim that words cannot produce error and cites Leibniz's anxiety about using words instead of ideas. Ribot's phrase: 'The word much resembles paper money' — useful but dangerous. Practical implication: beware of thinking that having the word suffices for understanding; test ideas beyond linguistic labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual fatigue stems from the effort of synthesis and schema construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual fatigue corresponds to the effort required to produce synthesis and to constitute a proper schema for the research problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author refers to physiological opinions (Lapicque) and psychological studies (Binet and Victor Henri) relating fatigue to the act of synthesizing; building the mental schema is effortful and produces fatigue distinct from mere physical activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant individual differences in cognitive style among thinkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive styles vary widely across individuals (visual, auditory, typographic-visual, symbolic), and one often cannot imagine how another person thinks; these differences impact comprehension between thinkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across mathematicians, composers, economists, and other scientists: some think without words, some with visual images, others in printed words. Historical consequences include resistance to novel ideas (Kronecker towards Cantor) possibly stemming from differing mental styles. Practical implication: don't assume universality of one's own cognitive mode; inquire rather than polemicize.
